title: The Granth's languages
hook: Punjabi, saint-speech, Braj and Persian voices, all in one script

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith and the state: kings are tigers, and the Gurus spoke plainly to the powerful. Your line was truth to rulers.

Open the Guru Granth Sahib and the letters look steady from page to page: one script, Gurmukhi, running down the lines. Read it aloud, though, and the sound keeps shifting. One hymn rolls in the Punjabi of village fields. A few pages on, a verse leans toward Persian, the language of courts and clerks. Another carries the old speech of wandering saint-poets. Same letters, different voices. A child who has learned the alphabet can sound out every line, and still meet words that traveled a long way to get there.
screen: `ONE SCRIPT ON EVERY PAGE.` → `READ ALOUD, THE SOUND SHIFTS.` → `MANY VOICES, ONE ALPHABET.`

segments.voice: First, the mix. Readers who study the Granth hear Punjabi in it, and the shared poetic speech of north Indian saints that scholars call Sant Bhasha, along with Braj, Persian and Arabic words, and verses that lean toward Sanskrit. The Gurus sang to the people in front of them, and those people spoke in more than one way. Second, one example. In Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak opens a hymn with yak arj guftam, words a Persian speaker would recognize: one plea I make before you. In paraphrase, he asks the Creator to listen, and says this world is passing. A prayer in the language of the court, set among hymns in the language of the village. Third, other voices. The Granth also holds the hymns of bhagats, saints from outside the line of the Gurus. Kabir calls himself a weaver. Sheikh Farid's sloks keep a Punjabi sound of their own. Their words were kept in their own speech, not smoothed into one. Fourth, the script. All of it is written in Gurmukhi. Tradition says Guru Angad shaped the script so ordinary people could read the hymns for themselves, with no one standing between them and the Word. So a child in a gurdwara class on a Sunday morning can sound out Persian, Braj and Punjabi alike. The voices stay different. The letters stay the same.
screen: `MANY SPEECHES ON ONE PAGE.` · `YAK ARJ GUFTAM: ONE PLEA BEFORE YOU.` · `THE BHAGATS KEEP THEIR OWN VOICES.` · `ONE SCRIPT ANYONE CAN LEARN.` · then, large: `MANY TONGUES, ONE SCRIPT.`

segments.voice: On one breath, say softly, or only in your mind, Kartar, the Creator, the name Guru Nanak calls on in his Tilang hymn; on the next, Khuda, a name for God a Persian speaker would know, which the Granth uses too; on the next, Hari, a name from older Indian devotional verse, which the hymns use too. Let the three sounds sit together, pointing the same way. If you pray, let them be your prayer; if you don't, just notice how each one feels in the mouth.
The Granth's languages. Punjabi, Persian, Braj and the speech of the saints, held in a single script, Gurmukhi. Today's word.
Your line: many tongues, one script. Words that traveled far, in letters a child can learn. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Sikhs learn to read Gurmukhi, often in gurdwara classes, so they can read the Guru Granth Sahib themselves, and the hymns are sung in their original words whatever language they lean toward.

chat.says: Is the Guru Granth Sahib all in one language, like Punjabi?
options: Not quite. It mixes Punjabi, Persian, Braj and more, all written in Gurmukhi.
Yes. It's all in Punjabi, the language the Gurus spoke at home.
No. It's mostly Sanskrit, written in a script only scholars can read.
chat.meaning: The Gurus sang to the people in front of them, in more than one tongue, and the bhagats kept their own speech. Gurmukhi holds it all in one script.
